new_statements.quote: The supra-segmental phonemes in Meitei are two tones. Length is not phonemic in this language.
new_statements.citation: Abbi, Anvita & Awadhesh K. Mishra. [1987]. Some Aspects of Meitei Phonology. 24 pp. ERIC document ED286374 (FL 016 924), section 1.2 'Supra-Segmental Phonemes'.
new_statements.locator: sec. 1.2, p. 4 (PDF page 4 of the ERIC microfiche scan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote verified on the page scan (page render of p. 4 of: section '1.2. Supra-Segmental Phonemes:' on printed page 4 reads exactly 'The supra-segmental phonemes in Meitei are two tones. Length is not phonemic in this language.' followed by Fig. 3 with columns HIGH / LOW. The text and the archive.org djvu text agree. A a full-text search for stress/accent the whole 24-page text finds no 'stress', 'accent' or 'prominence'; the paper is a phonemic inventory (20 consonants, 6 vowels, two tones) plus morpheme-structure rules and processes. Companion statement also verified on the page scan: Singh, Inder 1975 Manipuri Phonetic Reader p. 15 (p. 27): 'Suprasegmental sounds can be further classified…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Meithei is described by every accessible source as a lexical tone language with a two-way root tone contrast (high vs low; Bhat & Ningomba call it high-falling vs level; Inder Singh 1975 distinguishes three phonetic tones falling/rising/level); tone is a property of roots/syllables, affixes are toneless and take their pitch from the root (Chelliah 2003: 428). No accessible description states where word stress falls or whether stress exists as a separate prominence: Abbi & Mishra list tones as the only suprasegmental phonemes; Inder Singh 1975 (p. 15) names 'Tones, Stress and Intonation' as the suprasegmental categories but describes only tones; Chelliah 1990, 1997 (pp. 17-21), 2003 and Bhat & Ningomba 1997 never mention stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Companion statement, Singh, Inder 1975. Manipuri Phonetic Reader, p. 15: 'Suprasegmental sounds can be further classified into Tones Stress and Intonation. Tones are the only suprasegmentals which are discussed in this Reader. The domain of Tones are syllables in Manipuri.' Chelliah 1990: 98-99 notes that L2 vs L3 compounds 'may.. differ with regard to suprasegmental features. Further research will have to be conducted'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/root level: tone is lexically specified on roots (monosyllabic in native vocabulary) and spreads over affixed words by upstep/downstep (Chelliah 2003). Descriptions are of the Imphal standard dialect (Chelliah 2003: 427); Abbi & Mishra's data are from c. 40 speakers in Imphal. No source discusses citation-form vs phrase prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe standard (Imphal) Meithei = mani1292; Singh 1989 additionally describes the Kwatha village dialect (no separate glottocode known). Inder Singh 1975 analyses three tones (falling, rising, level) where Chelliah and Bhat & Ningomba analyse two; this is an analytic difference, not a variety difference. Bishnupriya Manipuri (Indo-Aryan) is a different language and was excluded.

new_statements.quote: Meiteilon is a tonal language which belongs to the Tibeto-Burman language family, predominantly spoken in Manipur. Various scholars offer different views with regard to the number and types of tones available in Meiteilon. Grierson (1904), Chelliah (1997) assert that Meiteilon has two register tones: high and low. [...] The researcher is also of the view that Meiteilon has two tones: High register tone and falling contour tone. [...] In this analysis the level tone is marked as ‘◌̄’ while the falling tone is marked as ‘◌̀’ above the vowel as nucleus is the tone bearing unit in Meiteilon.
new_statements.citation: Ningthoujam, Shyamkumar. 2017. A contrastive study of phonology in Chinese and Meiteilon. PhD thesis, Manipur University, Imphal (guide N. Pramodini Devi).
new_statements.locator: Chapter 4 'Syllables and tones of Chinese and Meiteilon', sec. 4.7 'Meiteilon Tones', pp. 188-189 (PDF pages 36-37 of; verified on rendered page scan). Scope remark: sec. 4.1, p. 153 (p. 1): 'the chapter deals with the challenges faced by the CFL learners in producing the Chinese syllables and lexical tones, leaving the other suprasegmental features such as intonation, juncture, etc. open for further studies.' Also ch. 1, p. 5: 'The language is tonal in nature which has two-way contrasts: level tone and high-low falling tone (Thoudam, 1980; Meiraba, 2014).'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (52 pp., created 12 Apr 2025). extracted text of pp. 36-37 (printed 188-189, footers visible) gives sec. '4.7. Meiteilon Tones' with every quoted sentence exactly as reported: 'Meiteilon is a tonal language which belongs to the Tibeto-Burman language family, predominantly spoken in Manipur. Various scholars offer different views with regard to the number and types of tones available in Meiteilon. Grierson (1904), Chelliah (1997) assert that Meiteilon has two register tones: high and low.'.. 'The researcher is also of the view that Meiteilon has two tones: High register tone and falling contour tone.'.. 'In this analysis the level tone is marked as ‘◌̄’ while the falling tone is marked…
new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog's existing statement (Abbi & Mishra 1987: 'two tones', no stress statement): tonal, two tones, nothing on stress. Adds detail: the two tones are analysed as high-level register vs falling contour (Abbi & Mishra give HIGH vs LOW), the vowel nucleus is the tone-bearing unit, and the author reviews the two-vs-three-tone disagreement. Does not add any placement or presence/absence statement for stress. The catalog year should read 2025 (registration 2017).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis treats Meiteilon as a tone language with two lexical tones on the syllable nucleus (high/level register tone vs falling contour tone, e.g. /i/ 'thatch' vs 'blood', /kʰoŋ/ 'canal' vs 'foot'); it makes no statement about word stress at all. A a full-text search for stress/accent every chapter for stress/accent/prominence finds only remarks on Kurdish and English in the literature review (ch. 1 p. 27) and 'native language accent' in the abstract. Suprasegmentals other than syllable structure and tone (intonation, juncture, etc.) are explicitly left for future work.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. On tone it reports a disagreement in the literature: Grierson 1904 and Chelliah 1997 give two register tones (high vs low), some scholars three (high, mid, low); Thoudam 1980, Devi 1989, Bhat & Ningomba 1997, Singh 2010, Meiraba 2014 and the author give high (level) vs falling (contour).
new_statements.identity_note: Ningthoujam describes standard Meiteilon as spoken by Manipur University students (Imphal, Manipur); no dialect is singled out. The thesis is a contrastive study of Mandarin Chinese and Meiteilon for Chinese-as-a-foreign-language pedagogy; the Chinese material is not about this language.

tone_statements.quote: This paper is a description of the tone system of the Tibeto-Burman language Manipuri (also known as Meiteiron or Meithei, hereafter referred to as M). I will present evidence that M exhibits a two way tonal contrast between a lexically marked low (L) tone and a default high (H) tone. ... Minimal pairs such as those listed in Table 1, establish the existence of a H and L tone for stems and bound roots ... Whereas Manipuri stems have either H or L tone, suffixes are unspecified for tone at both an underlying and surface level.
tone_statements.summary: Stems/roots contrast lexical L vs default H; suffixes toneless (pitch = transition to boundary tones H%, L%); author: near pitch accent but 'don't quite make it'. F0 of 284 tokens.

tone_statements.citation: Ashem, Reena. 2018. Prosodic words in Meiteilon: morpho-syntactic influence on morpho-phonological well-formedness. PhD thesis, Department of Humanities and Social Sciences, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi (supervisor Paroma Sanyal). Shodhganga hdl 10603/562457.
tone_statements.quote: Manipuri is a syllabic register-tone language. Tonemes are always placed on the vowel of the syllable. There are two tone groups, viz. Primary tone and Secondary tone. Primary tones are the basic tones and secondary tones are the allotone. ... Then, the Primary tones are again classified into two ; such as level tone and falling tone. ... There is distinction between level and falling tones on monosyllabic words. ... Manipuri being a tonic language, the difference in meaning is generated by the change in tone. Manipuri has only two tones – level and falling.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 6.4.1 p. 261; sec. 6.4.2 p. 262; ch. 7 (b) Supra-Segmentals p. 277
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, level vs falling (author calls it a 'register-tone language'); minimal pairs credited to Madhubala 2002; disyllables show FF/FL/LF/LL; prefixes copy root tone; L>F / F>L spreading rules.

tone_statements.summary: 2 tones: level vs falling (acoustic study, isolated tonal minimal pairs).

tone_statements.quote: Manipuri is a tone language. It has lexically significant, contrastive but relative pitch on each syllable. ... In confirmity with the perceptual observation, the limited study of instrumental verification suggests that there are only two distinctive tones namely, falling tone, marked as /ˋ/ and level tone unmarked in the transcription. The tone is marked over the vowel in a syllable. ... Phonetically, there are three tones namely, level, fall and rise-fall, whereas phonemically it is possible to establish only two tones ...
tone_statements.summary: Two tonemes: falling vs level (unmarked); level has a rise-fall allotone after a falling syllable; 1983 spectrograms of 4 pairs, called limited.

tone.quote: To determine whether the two seemingly homophonous verb roots behave exactly the same, these words were recorded in PRAAT. ... Thus, the above phonetic data illustrates that a pitch distinction is present between the two seeming homophonous roots. Since Meiteilon is a tonal language, I argue that the presence of this distinct pitch pattern indicates the two verbal roots are indeed different.

tone.says: 'Manipuri is a low-resource Tibeto-Burman tonal language.. This thesis presents the development of a meticulously crafted speech corpus called ManiTo, explicitly designed to analyze the tones of Manipuri. Comprising 17,837 labeled audio samples from twenty native speakers.. Initial investigations reveal the presence of two distinct tones: Falling and Level. A comprehensive acoustic feature analysis was conducted to differentiate between the two tones' (pitch contour, jitter, shimmer features; S…

tone.quote: Manipuri is a tone language. It has lexically significant, contrastive but relative pitch on each syllable. ... In confirmity with the perceptual observation, the limited study of instrumental verification suggests that there are only two distinctive tones namely, falling tone, marked as /ˋ/ and level tone unmarked in the transcription. The tone is marked over the vowel in a syllable. ... Phonetically, there are three tones namely, level, fall and rise-fall, whereas phonemically it is possible to establish only two tones ...
tone.summary: Two tonemes: falling vs level (unmarked); level has a rise-fall allotone after a falling syllable; 1983 spectrograms of 4 pairs, called limited.
